Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

there are about fourteen regular members, with a different number turning up each week. mina, who organizes most walks, knows a lot about bird calls and is patient when people ask the same question twice. on my first morning she said, “we'll take the route slowly, and nobody has to identify everything.” that turned out to be a good description of the group. people share what they know, but there is no pressure to sound like an expert. i had only used binoculars at a zoo before, and mina showed me how to adjust the focus without taking the pair out of my hands. The group has four loan pairs, and they can be reserved by email; two were available when i first came.

The membership is $25 for a year, and a first-time guest can attend two walks without paying. That seemed fair to me, especially since the group sends a short monthly email with meeting points and recent sightings. the email is useful, although the map link for the canal walk led me to the wrong bridge once. i checked the street signs and found everyone after a few minutes, but it would help if the start point were written out as well as shown on the map. mina apologized when i mentioned it and said she would look at the link. i don't know whether it has been changed since then.

1. things i liked

The walks have helped me notice ordinary places in a different way. On the rail embankment, we watched a pair of blackbirds feeding near a fence and then spent several minutes listening for a chiffchaff. At the hospital garden, one member pointed out a nest box fixed above a bench, and we watched from the path instead of going closer. The group keeps a respectful distance from nests and does not use recorded calls to attract birds. I appreciated that, because i had assumed birding meant getting close enough for a photograph. nobody treated a missed sighting as a failure; when we did not find the kingfisher at the canal, mina talked about the water level and where it might be feeding instead.

The pace is accessible for most of the people i have walked with. There are benches on two of the routes, and mina tells the group in advance when a path has steps or a muddy stretch. The hospital garden route is nearly flat, but the rail embankment has one short slope that was slippery after rain. People waited while i took it slowly, and no one made me feel that i was holding them up. Newcomers are introduced by first name, though not everyone remembers names immediately. A printed one-page list of common local birds is available at the indoor meeting, which was helpful because i remember pictures better than Latin names.

There are a couple of less comfortable parts. The canal towpath becomes narrow near the lock, and when the group is spread out, people sometimes talk loudly across the path. A cyclist rang a bell behind us on my third walk, and we moved aside, but the moment felt avoidable. I think it would be better to gather at the wider landing before discussing a sighting. Attendance is uneven, too: once only five people came, while the hospital garden walk had eleven. The smaller group was quieter and easier to hear, but it also meant there were fewer people to share binoculars and point out birds.

At the indoor meeting, held in a room above the library, we looked at members' photographs and talked through a simple checklist for reporting sightings. It lasted an hour and a half, with tea in paper cups and no formal presentation. One member said, “i used to think the gulls were all the same,” and several people laughed because they had said something similar when they started. I liked the relaxed atmosphere, although the room was warm and the chairs were close together. The meeting is not required for membership, and nobody suggested that people should attend every event.

I would recommend the east quay bird circle to someone who is curious about city wildlife and comfortable being outdoors early. It suits beginners better than people looking for a highly structured course, in my experience. I still mix up a few calls, and i am not sure i would manage the names without the printed list, but i enjoy the walks and the company.
